checkpoint.prompt: What is the one-sentence frame this course runs on?
choices: Whatever we are to each other, we are one team for the child
Keep the peace at any cost
Win the important decisions

checkpoint.prompt: Being one team requires what, per this session?
choices: Being friends with the other parent
Agreeing on everything
Working the child's interests together, whatever the history between you

checkpoint.prompt: What does the child gain when the team holds?
choices: Two households pulling one direction, which lowers the load they carry
Fewer rules
A guarantee of no conflict

checkpoint.prompt: What do you write in this session?
choices: A long parenting agreement
One child-centered sentence you can both hold
A list of past grievances

checkpoint.prompt: Which sentence is child-centered?
choices: We keep school nights calm so she can sleep and learn.
You need to admit what you did.
We will never disagree again.

checkpoint.prompt: Why one sentence instead of many?
choices: Courts prefer short documents
One clear goal steers hard moments; a stack of demands restarts the fight
Children cannot understand long goals

checkpoint.prompt: What does flooded mean in this session?
choices: Being sad
Your body so activated that judgment is gone; continuing makes it worse
Disagreeing strongly

checkpoint.prompt: What is the rule when you notice you are flooded?
choices: Push through to resolution
Pause, about twenty minutes, then resume
End all contact for the week

checkpoint.prompt: Why twenty minutes, roughly?
choices: It is how long the body needs to actually come down; five minutes of silent rehearsing does not count
It is a rule of the platform
It gives you time to build your case

checkpoint.prompt: What belongs in a clean break?
choices: A long speech about why you are leaving
A short line that names the pause and when you will resume
Silence and a hung-up call

checkpoint.prompt: Which line is a clean break?
choices: I am flooded. Let's resume at 8 tonight.
I am done with you.
Fine. Whatever.

checkpoint.prompt: Why name when you will resume?
choices: So the other parent feels controlled
So the pause is a reset, not abandonment of the topic
So you can skip the topic forever

checkpoint.prompt: What are the three marks of businesslike communication here?
choices: Short, factual, about the child
Polite, warm, frequent
Written, formal, copied to others

checkpoint.prompt: Which message is businesslike?
choices: Pickup Friday is 5:30 at school; she has her science fair board with her.
We need to talk about your choices lately.
Fine. Whatever works for you, as usual.

checkpoint.prompt: Why keep it to the child?
choices: Because the old disputes are settled
Because every message that stays on the child is one that cannot reopen the marriage
Because feelings are wrong

checkpoint.prompt: What does this session ask you to choose?
choices: The channel that lowers heat
The channel that wins arguments
Only face-to-face conflict

checkpoint.prompt: When a text thread heats up, the cooler move is often?
choices: Keep typing faster
Move to a written log or a scheduled call after a pause
Bring the child into the thread

checkpoint.prompt: Why channel choice matters?
choices: Some apps are free
The medium can raise or lower heat before a word is read
Courts ban all texts

checkpoint.prompt: What buys back a co-parent's trust, per this session?
choices: Reliability, kept small promises, over time
A sincere conversation about the past
Generosity with money

checkpoint.prompt: Which is the right first promise to rebuild with?
choices: A large one, to prove commitment
A small one you are certain to keep, then another
None; let time do it

checkpoint.prompt: You were late last week. The rebuild move is?
choices: Explain at length
Be early to the next three agreed times without a speech
Skip the next handoff

checkpoint.prompt: How does this session treat court orders and agreements?
choices: As obstacles to work around when unfair
As the floor you never build against; trust is earned inside them, never against them
As relevant only to lawyers

checkpoint.prompt: What must you never ask a child to carry?
choices: A backpack
An adult fight
A school folder

checkpoint.prompt: Which action fits this session?
choices: Keep every commitment exactly as written inside the order
Ask the child to pass a message about money
Skip a visit to make a point

checkpoint.prompt: Who carries the distance between two homes, per this session?
choices: The parents equally
The child; your job is to lighten the load
Nobody, if the schedule is fair

checkpoint.prompt: Which lightens the child's load?
choices: Asking what happens at the other house to gather ammo
Letting the child feel free to love both homes out loud
Keeping the households completely identical

checkpoint.prompt: Your child praises something at the other home. The session's move is what?
choices: Receive it warmly; their ease is the win
Match it with something better at yours
Change the subject

checkpoint.prompt: What beats perfect agreement, per this session?
choices: Predictable rules
Identical houses
No rules at either home

checkpoint.prompt: Which helps a child across two homes?
choices: Fighting until every rule matches
A few clear, predictable rules the child can count on at your place
Asking the child to choose a side

checkpoint.prompt: Why predictability matters more than perfection?
choices: Courts require it
A child can adapt to two homes when each home is steady
Children dislike agreement

checkpoint.prompt: What is the standard for handoffs in this session?
choices: Predictable beats perfect
Quick beats friendly
Flexible beats scheduled

checkpoint.prompt: What belongs at a handoff?
choices: The unresolved topic from last week
The child's things, the practical facts, a calm goodbye
A private word with the other parent about concerns

checkpoint.prompt: Why does predictability matter so much at the handoff moment?
choices: It saves time
The handoff is where the child feels the team most directly; calm sameness tells them the ground is solid
It prevents lateness

checkpoint.prompt: What is the handoff ritual built from?
choices: Same place, same time, same calm script
Surprise locations to keep it fresh
Long talks at every exchange

checkpoint.prompt: Which script fits the ritual?
choices: Bag, jacket, homework. See you Thursday at 5.
We need to talk about last month right now.
Tell your mother what I said.

checkpoint.prompt: Why keep the ritual short and same?
choices: So adults can argue later elsewhere
Sameness lowers the child's stress at the transition
Children prefer silence always

final_qa.prompt: Write the last message you sent the other parent, then rewrite it businesslike: short, factual, about the child. What changed?
Describe one flooded moment this course caught: where you felt it, how you paused, and what resuming later made possible.
Name the small promise you are using to rebuild trust inside the agreement that governs you, and your record of keeping it so far.
Write your handoff ritual in four lines: place, time, calm script, and what never gets discussed at the exchange.
